## Preface

The primary goal of Open Source Football is to make football analysis and the
code behind it publicly available. To achieve this, we need volunteers who are
willing to contribute.

Posts are written with [Quarto](https://quarto.org) in **R or Python** (or any
other language Quarto supports). If something in this guide is unclear or wrong,
please [open an issue](https://github.com/nflverse/open-source-football/issues/new).

## Overview

1. Fork and clone the repository, and create a branch.
2. Copy a post template to `posts/YYYY-MM-DD-short-title/`.
3. Write your post.
4. Render it locally. This runs your code once and stores the results in `_freeze/`.
5. Commit your post folder **and** `_freeze/`, then open a pull request.

We will review the post, suggest changes if necessary, and publish it by
merging the pull request.

## 1. Fork, clone, and branch

You need [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/) (≥ 1.7), git, and
the language you write in: for R, the `rmarkdown` and `knitr` packages; for
Python, `jupyter`.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R (usethis)

```r
usethis::create_from_github("nflverse/open-source-football")
usethis::pr_init(branch = "my-post-title")
```

## GitHub CLI

The repository has a long history. `--filter=blob:none` makes the clone much
smaller and faster.

```sh
gh repo fork nflverse/open-source-football --clone -- --filter=blob:none
cd open-source-football
git switch -c my-post-title
```
:::

## 2. Copy a template

Copy the R or the Python template and give the folder a date-prefixed,
descriptive name:

```sh
cp -r _post_template posts/2026-01-15-my-post-title          # R
cp -r _post_template_python posts/2026-01-15-my-post-title   # Python
```

## 3. Write your post

Open `posts/2026-01-15-my-post-title/index.qmd`, fill in the metadata (title,
description, author, date, categories), and write. The template shows the
basics. Please keep in mind:

- **Readers should be able to rerun your code years later.** Load data from
  public sources such as [nflreadr](https://nflreadr.nflverse.com) or
  [nflreadpy](https://github.com/nflverse/nflreadpy), not from local files.
  Don't commit large data files.
- **Keep the *Session info* section** at the end of the template. It records
  the package versions you used. You don't need renv or a lockfile.
- The first figure becomes the preview image on the home page. To pick a
  different one, set `image:` in the metadata to a file in your post folder.
- Use `#| column: page` on cells with wide figures or tables.
- The site has a light and a dark mode. Figures with a white background work
  in both.

## 4. Render

```sh
quarto render posts/2026-01-15-my-post-title/index.qmd
```

This runs your code and writes the results to `_freeze/`. The website build
reuses these frozen results and **never runs your code itself**, so your post
keeps working even when data or packages change later. If you edit the post
afterwards, render it again.

To see the post in the site while you write, use `quarto preview` with the same
path instead.

## 5. Commit and open a pull request

Commit your post folder and everything new in `_freeze/` (your results, plus
any JavaScript and CSS of interactive widgets such as plotly in
`_freeze/site_libs/`). Don't commit the `_site/` folder.

```sh
git add posts/2026-01-15-my-post-title _freeze
git commit -m "Add post: My post title"
```

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R (usethis)

```r
usethis::pr_push()
```

## GitHub CLI

```sh
git push -u origin my-post-title
gh pr create
```
:::

A check on your pull request builds the whole site. It fails if `_freeze/` is
missing or older than your post; render again and commit to fix it (you can run
the same check locally with `_scripts/check-freeze.sh`). The rendered site is
attached to the check as a downloadable `site-preview` artifact.

That's it. Thanks for your contribution!
